l: Jordan, The Second Book of Samuel
s: David and all his people passed over the Jordan by morning light, with none left behind. Afterward Absalom and all the men of Israel also crossed it.

l: Bethlehem, The Second Book of Samuel
s: has_part well of Bethlehem [by the gate] Bethlehem is held by a Philistine garrison while David is in the stronghold. David longs for water from its well by the gate. Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem is listed among the thirty.

l: Saul’s house, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Saul's house is a royal household that weakens during a long war with David's house, as its strongman Abner vows to transfer the kingdom to David. Later David shows kindness, and Mephibosheth, the remaining member, receives all Saul's holdings.

l: David’s house, The Second Book of Samuel
s: grows stronger [during the long war with Saul’s house] David's house grows stronger and stronger in the war against Saul's house. It gains an expectation that all Israel will come over to David through Abner's covenant effort, though Abner's death interrupts it.

l: Michal, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Michal, Saul's daughter, once married to Paltiel, watches David's ark procession and despises him for dancing. She confronts him, he rebuts her, and she remains childless until her death.

l: Rizpah, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Rizpah, daughter of Aiah and Saul's concubine, mothers Armoni and Mephibosheth, both hanged. She spreads sackcloth on the rock and guards their bodies from birds and animals from harvest until rain, and David is told.

l: Amnon, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Amnon, David's son, desires his half-sister Tamar, tricks her into coming to him via Jonadab's plan, rapes her, then hates her more than he loved her and has her bolted out. Two years later Absalom's servants kill him at a sheep shearing.

l: Absalom, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Absalom is a son of David, celebrated as the most beautiful man in all Israel, with no defect and heavy hair cut yearly. He has three sons and a daughter, Tamar. His story begins when he hates Amnon for forcing Tamar. After two years of silence he invites the king's sons to a sheep shearing, persuades David to let Amnon come, and has his servants kill Amnon when merry with wine. He flees to Talmai, king of Geshur, and stays three years. Joab brings him back to Jerusalem, but he must live in his own house without seeing the king. After two years he has Joab's field burned to gain attention, says he would rather be dead than kept from the king, and bows before David, who kisses him. Absalom then prepares a chariot, horses and fifty runners, and wins the hearts of Israelites at the gate by promising justice. Under the pretext of a vow he goes to Hebron, sends spies to proclaim himself king, and summons Ahithophel. The people anoint him king. He enters Jerusalem, tests Hushai's loyalty, follows Ahithophel's counsel by going in to his father's concubines in sight of all Israel, then favors Hushai's counsel. He crosses the Jordan, camps in Gilead, and sets Amasa over the army instead of Joab. In battle, riding his mule in the forest, he is caught by his head in an oak. Joab thrusts darts through his heart and ten armor-bearers kill him. He is thrown into a pit under a heap of stones. Having no son to keep his name, he had raised a pillar, still called Absalom's monument. David mourns him bitterly, while Joab rebukes David for loving him over all others.

l: Abner's murder, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Joab, aided by his brother Abishai, kills Abner at Hebron's gate to avenge Asahel. David, unaware beforehand, declares himself guiltless, curses Joab's house, and leads public mourning, convincing all Israel he did not will it.

l: Baanah, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Baanah, a Benjamite Beerothite, son of Rimmon and raiding-band captain under Ishbosheth, kills him with brother Rechab, brings the head to David claiming divine vengeance, and is executed on David's order.

l: Rechab, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Rechab, a Benjamite Beerothite and son of Rimmon, captains a raiding band under Ishbosheth; he and Baanah murder Ishbosheth and bring his head to David, who executes and hangs him at Hebron.

l: Mephibosheth, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Mephibosheth is the lame-footed son of Jonathan and grandson of Saul, father of a young son, Mica. Living in Lo Debar at Machir's house, he is summoned by David, bows as a 'dead dog', and is promised Saul's land and a permanent place at the king's table in Jerusalem. Later, Ziba reports he is staying in Jerusalem hoping Israel will restore his father's kingdom, so David gives Ziba all his property. When Mephibosheth meets David, unkempt in mourning, he says Ziba deceived and slandered him. David orders the land divided; Mephibosheth says Ziba may take all, since the king has returned in peace.

l: murder of Ishbosheth, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Rechab and Baanah murder Ishbosheth on his bed in his own house at midday, entering under pretense of fetching wheat. They behead him, flee overnight via the Arabah, and bring his head to David in Hebron, claiming the LORD's vengeance.

l: execution of Rechab and Baanah, The Second Book of Samuel
s: David orders the execution of Rechab and Baanah, condemning them for killing a righteous man in his bed; his young men kill them, cut off their hands and feet, and hang the bodies beside Hebron's pool.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Jerusalem is where David reigns thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah. David takes more concubines and wives from there, and the sons born to him there are named, including Solomon. Jerusalem was the city David fled, fearing Absalom might strike it with the sword, leaving ten concubines to keep the house. The ark was returned there with Zadok and Abiathar, Hushai went in as David's friend, and Absalom entered it at the end of the unit.

l: Jebusites, The Second Book of Samuel
s: inhabit Jerusalem [inhabitants of the land] The Jebusites, inhabitants of the land, taunt David that the blind and the lame will keep him out of Jerusalem. David nonetheless takes their stronghold of Zion, and he calls for those lame and blind, hated by his soul, to be struck.

l: Zion, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Zion, a stronghold the Jebusites boasted David could not enter, is captured by David and renamed David's city. He lives there, pauses moving the ark after Uzzah's death, then brings it in joyfully and offers sacrifices.

l: Nathan, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Nathan is a prophet and advisor to King David, sent by the LORD. He first tells David to follow his heart, then is corrected by the LORD's word and delivers the message about the house and promises. Later he confronts David's sin with a parable, declares "You are the man!", announces judgment, and conveys Solomon's naming as Jedidiah.

l: Solomon, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Solomon, son of David and Bathsheba born after the first child's death, is loved by the LORD and named Jedidiah through Nathan.

l: David's covenant with the elders, The Second Book of Samuel
s: made_at Hebron [before the LORD] King David makes a covenant with all the elders of Israel at Hebron before the LORD. After it, they anoint him king over Israel.

l: Battle at Baal Perazim, The Second Book of Samuel
s: David's battle against the Philistines at Baal Perazim: the LORD instructs him and promises delivery, David strikes them, likens it to breaching waters, names the place, and carries off their abandoned images.

l: ark of the covenant of God, The Second Book of Samuel
s: The ark of God, called by the Name of the LORD of Armies enthroned above the cherubim, is moved on a new cart from Abinadab's house, stumbles at Nacon's threshing floor, and after Uzzah's death rests three months with Obed-Edom before entering David's city and his tent.

l: Uzzah, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Uzzah, a son of Abinadab, drives the new cart with his brother Ahio. When the cattle stumble, he reaches out and takes hold of the ark, and God strikes him dead there for his error.

l: Obed-Edom, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Obed-Edom, a Gittite, takes the ark into his house after David fears moving it; the LORD blesses him, his household, and all he owns for three months.

l: chosen men of Israel, The Second Book of Samuel
s: has_quality mighty and valiant [per Hushai] The people with David were described as hungry, weary and thirsty in the wilderness. They crossed the Jordan with him by morning with none lacking, and were fed at Mahanaim with provisions brought by Shobi, Machir and Barzillai.

l: Uzzah's death, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Uzzah dies at Nacon's threshing floor when the LORD strikes him for his error after he grips the ark to steady it. David, displeased and afraid, names the place Perez Uzzah and leaves the ark at Obed-Edom's house.

l: David's dancing, The Second Book of Samuel
s: performed_by David [before the LORD, with all his might] David dances before the LORD with all his might, clothed in a linen ephod, as the ark is brought up with shouting and trumpets. Michal despises it and calls it shameless, but David defends it as celebration before the LORD and says he will be even more undignified.

l: house for God's name (temple), The Second Book of Samuel
s: will_be_built_by David's offspring (David's son) David's wish to replace the ark's curtains with a house prompts the LORD's reply that he never asked anyone for a cedar house. The LORD declares that David's offspring will build a house for his name, and he will establish the throne of that son's kingdom forever.

l: David's dynasty (house of David), The Second Book of Samuel
s: has_duration forever [house and kingdom made sure] The LORD promises that he will make David a house, and that David's house and kingdom will be made sure forever, with his throne established forever. David in his prayer asks God to confirm this promise and bless his house so that it continues forever before him.

l: David's offspring (David's son), The Second Book of Samuel
s: David's promised offspring, raised up by the LORD after David sleeps with his fathers. He will build a house for the LORD's name, with the LORD as his father and an eternally established throne. Iniquity brings chastening with men's rod, yet lovingkindness never departs, unlike with Saul.

l: enemies (David's enemies), The Second Book of Samuel
s: David's enemies, including a strong foe who hated him and Saul, attack in his calamity, too mighty only for David alone. With the LORD's help he pursues and crushes them; unanswered when they cry to the LORD, they fall, and foreigners come trembling to submit.

l: David's prayer, The Second Book of Samuel
s: David's prayer to the LORD in Chapter 7: humbled, he asks who he is, praises God's greatness and Israel's redemption from Egypt, then asks that the promise about his house be confirmed and blessed forever, since God revealed it to him.

l: Moab, The Second Book of Samuel
s: is_servant_of David [brings tribute] David defeated Moab and measured them with a line, making them lie on the ground; two lines' worth were put to death and one full line kept alive. The Moabites became servants to David and brought tribute.

l: Hadadezer, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Hadadezer, son of Rehob, is king of Zobah and lord over servant kings, owning the cities Betah and Berothai. He was at war with Toi. David struck him as he sought to recover his dominion at the River, capturing horsemen, footmen, shields and bronze. He then summoned Syrians from beyond the River under Shobach; defeated at Helam, his servant kings made peace with Israel and served them.

l: Syrians of Damascus, The Second Book of Samuel
s: is_servant_of David [brings tribute] The Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadadezer, and David struck twenty-two thousand of them. David then put garrisons in Syria of Damascus, and the Syrians became his servants and brought tribute.

l: children of Ammon, The Second Book of Samuel
s: The children of Ammon are a people ruled by Hanun, with princes who persuaded him that David's envoys were spies. Having become odious to David, they hired Syrian, Maacah and Tob troops but fled before Abishai. Later David conquered Rabbah, took the king's crown, and forced the people into labor.

l: Edom, The Second Book of Samuel
s: is_servant_of David [Edomites] David put garrisons throughout all Edom, and all the Edomites became his servants. The LORD gave David victory wherever he went.

l: Zadok, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Zadok, son of Ahitub and father of Ahimaaz, is a priest David calls a seer. He brings the ark with the Levites, is told to carry it back, and is named a recipient of Hushai's reports.

l: Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Benaiah, son of Jehoiada and of a valiant man of Kabzeel, commanded the Cherethites and Pelethites. He killed Ariel of Moab's two sons, a lion in a pit, and a huge Egyptian with the man's own spear. Ranked above the thirty but below the three, he was set by David over his guard.

l: Ziba, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Ziba is a servant of Saul's house with fifteen sons and twenty servants. He tells David about Jonathan's lame son, and David orders his household to till Saul's land for Mephibosheth, making them Mephibosheth's servants. Later, Ziba meets the fleeing David with donkeys and provisions, says Mephibosheth is staying in Jerusalem hoping to regain his father's kingdom, and receives all Mephibosheth's property from David, bowing and asking for favor.

l: land (Mephibosheth and Ziba), The Second Book of Samuel
s: David promises to restore all of Saul's land to Mephibosheth and declares that all that belonged to Saul and his house is given to him. Ziba, his sons and his servants are to till it and bring in the harvest so that Mephibosheth has bread.

l: kindness, The Second Book of Samuel
s: David wants to show kindness for Jonathan's sake, which he also calls the kindness of God. He carries it out by restoring Saul's land to Mephibosheth and giving him a continual place at the king's table.

l: king's table, The Second Book of Samuel
s: David promises that Mephibosheth will eat bread at his table continually, and this is repeated in the unit. Mephibosheth lives in Jerusalem because he eats there continually, like one of the king's sons.

l: Hanun, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Hanun, son of Nahash, succeeds his father as king of the Ammonites; swayed by his princes to suspect David's comforters as spies, he humiliates David's servants by shaving beards and cutting garments, becoming David's enemy.

l: Syrians, The Second Book of Samuel
s: is_afraid_to_help children of Ammon [after defeat] The Syrians of Beth Rehob and Zobah, along with the king of Maacah and the men of Tob, were hired by the Ammonites and fled before Joab. They regrouped under Hadadezer at Helam, were defeated by David, and afterward were afraid to help the Ammonites any more.

l: Shobach, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Shobach, captain of Hadadezer's army, led the Syrians at Helam, where David struck him and he died.

l: battle against Ammon and Syrians, The Second Book of Samuel
s: has_outcome Israel victorious [Ammon and Syrians fled] Joab and Abishai fought in two divisions at the Ammonite city gate, with the Syrians in the field, and both enemy forces fled. The Syrians regathered under Hadadezer and were beaten again at Helam by David, ending with peace from Hadadezer's servant kings and Syrian reluctance to aid Ammon.

l: Bathsheba, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam and very beautiful wife of Uriah the Hittite, is taken by David and conceives. After mourning Uriah she becomes David's wife and bears a son, whom the LORD strikes and who dies. David comforts her, and she then bears Solomon.

l: Uriah the Hittite, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Uriah the Hittite is a loyal soldier, one of the thirty, who serves Joab. Summoned from war by David, he refuses the comfort of home while the ark, Israel, Judah and Joab's men camp in the open. Unwittingly carrying the letter ordering his death, he is killed near the city wall by the Ammonites' sword. Nathan later names David as his killer, grounding the LORD's charge.

l: Rabbah, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Rabbah is the walled Ammonite royal city, the city of waters. Joab besieges it, and Uriah dies fighting near its wall. David orders the assault, then captures it: its crown is taken, plunder carried off, and its people put to labor.

l: letter (David's letter to Joab), The Second Book of Samuel
s: A letter written by David to Joab, carried by Uriah himself, ordering Joab to place Uriah at the front of the hottest battle, then retreat from him so he is struck down and dies.

l: war against Ammon, The Second Book of Samuel
s: War against Ammon: David sends Joab and all Israel, who destroy the Ammonites and besiege Rabbah; during the siege, men of the city sally out and shoot from the wall, killing David's servants and Uriah.

l: rich man (Nathan's parable), The Second Book of Samuel
s: possesses flocks and herds [very many] In Nathan's parable the rich man has very many flocks and herds. When a traveler comes, he spares his own animals and takes the poor man's lamb to prepare for the guest. David declares that this man deserves to die and must restore fourfold.

l: poor man (Nathan's parable), The Second Book of Samuel
s: possesses ewe lamb (the poor man's lamb) [his only possession] In the parable the poor man has nothing but one little ewe lamb that he bought and raised. His lamb is taken by the rich man to feed a traveler.

l: ewe lamb (the poor man's lamb), The Second Book of Samuel
s: is_like daughter [to the poor man] The ewe lamb grew up with the poor man and his children, ate his food, drank from his cup, lay in his bosom, and was like a daughter to him. The rich man takes it and prepares it for a traveler.

l: child (David and Bathsheba's first son), The Second Book of Samuel
s: The child born to David and Uriah's wife is struck by the LORD and becomes very sick, as Nathan foretold. He dies on the seventh day, despite David's fasting and pleading.

l: David's sin (adultery and murder), The Second Book of Samuel
s: has_consequence sword never departing from David's house [decreed by the LORD] Nathan charges that David despised the LORD's word by killing Uriah the Hittite and taking his wife. The LORD declares the sword will never leave David's house and that his wives will be taken and given to his neighbor publicly. David confesses, and his sin is put away so he will not die, though the child will because it gave the LORD's enemies occasion to blaspheme.

l: David's fasting and mourning for the child, The Second Book of Samuel
s: lasts seven days [until the child died] While the child lives, David begs God, fasts, weeps, and lies all night on the ground, refusing the elders' efforts to raise him. After the child dies, he washes, changes clothes, worships in the LORD's house, and eats, explaining that he can't bring the child back but will go to him.

l: Israelite army (the people), The Second Book of Samuel
s: David's people were set under captains and went out in three divisions, but they persuaded David not to go with them, saying he was worth ten thousand of them. They heard the king's command to deal gently with Absalom, fought in the forest of Ephraim, and returned from the pursuit when Joab blew the trumpet.

l: Tamar, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Tamar, Absalom's beautiful virgin sister, is sent by David to make cakes at Amnon's house. She resists his advances and urges him to ask the king, but he rapes her and casts her out. She mourns publicly, then lives desolate in Absalom's house.

l: Jonadab, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Jonadab, son of Shimeah and nephew of David, is Amnon's friend, called very subtle. He counsels Amnon to feign sickness to get Tamar sent, then after the killing tells David only Amnon died, per Absalom's design, and announces the sons' return.

l: rape of Tamar, The Second Book of Samuel
s: victim Tamar Amnon forces Tamar after luring her into his room under pretense of illness, ignoring her protest that it is a folly not done in Israel. He then hates her and expels her, which she calls a wrong worse than the first. The act leaves Tamar desolate, angers David, and is the stated reason for Absalom's hatred and Amnon's later death.

l: murder of Amnon, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Amnon's murder is revenge for his rape of Tamar: after two years Absalom has servants kill him at a wine-merry sheep shearing, a false report claims all sons died until Jonadab corrects it, and Absalom flees to Geshur while David mourns.

l: woman of Tekoa, The Second Book of Samuel
s: The wise woman of Tekoa, sent by Joab and coached to pose as a mourner, tells the king a story of her two sons, wins his oath, then argues he is guilty for not recalling his banished one, finally admitting Joab's role.

l: son who killed his brother (widow's son), The Second Book of Samuel
s: is_brother_of slain brother (widow's son) [killed him in a field fight] In the woman's story, this son struck his brother in a field with no one to part them and killed him. The family demands his handing over to be killed, which would destroy the heir. The king swears that not a hair of his head will fall to the earth.

l: the widow's story of the two sons, The Second Book of Samuel
s: A fabricated plea Joab put in a widow's mouth: her two sons fought, one killed the other, and the family demands the killer's death, which would end her husband's name and remainder. The king promises the surviving son protection. She then applies this to his banished son, and the king recognizes Joab behind it.

l: Absalom's banishment and return, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Absalom's banishment in Geshur ends when the king has Joab bring him to Jerusalem, but the return is partial: he lives in his own house, barred from the king's face for two years. Joab then carries his plea, and the king receives his bow and kisses him.

l: Ahithophel, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Ahithophel, from Giloh, is a counselor whose advice was esteemed as if inquired of God's inner sanctuary, serving both David and Absalom. He joins Absalom's conspiracy, and David prays that his counsel become foolishness. He advises Absalom to go in to David's concubines, then to let him pursue David with twelve thousand men that night and strike only the king. When his counsel is not followed, he goes home, sets his house in order, hangs himself, and is buried in his father's tomb.

l: Hushai the Archite, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Hushai the Archite is a friend of David who appears as a double-agent figure in the records. Meeting David on the Mount of Olives in mourning, he is told he would be a burden and is sent instead to serve Absalom, defeat Ahithophel's counsel, and report to the priests Zadok and Abiathar. He enters the city, pledges allegiance to Absalom, declaring he will serve whom the LORD and people choose. He then argues Ahithophel's advice is poor, urging a full gathering of Israel; Absalom accepts it, and Hushai warns David through the priests.

l: Ittai the Gittite, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Ittai, a Gittite from Gath described by David as a foreigner and exile, refuses David's offer to turn back, swears loyalty in life or death, crosses over with his men and families, and commands a third of David's people.

l: Ahimaaz, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Ahimaaz, son of Zadok, is a swift-running messenger judged a good man by David. With Jonathan he waited at En Rogel, hid in a well at Bahurim, escaped Absalom's servants, and warned David that Ahithophel had counseled against him. Later he insisted on running news to David despite Joab's refusal, outran the Cushite, was recognized by his running, reported all well, but claimed ignorance about Absalom.

l: Absalom's conspiracy, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Absalom's conspiracy is a rebellion he leads, built through gate-side courting, tribal spies, and unknowing invitees from Jerusalem. It strengthens when David's counselor Ahithophel joins and people keep increasing, forcing David to flee. Absalom enters Jerusalem, receives Hushai's pledge and counsel, and publicly takes his father's concubines.

l: concubines (David's ten concubines), The Second Book of Samuel
s: keeps David [left to keep the house] David's concubines, whom he left to keep the house, are the object of Ahithophel's advice. Absalom goes in to them on a tent on the top of the house in the sight of all Israel.

l: David's flight from Jerusalem, The Second Book of Samuel
s: is_caused_by Absalom's conspiracy [hearts of Israel's men follow Absalom] David ordered his servants to flee at once to avoid being overtaken and the city struck, and the king's household and people followed him out, crossing the Kidron toward the wilderness. Along the way Ittai pledged loyalty, the ark was sent back, and David went up the Mount of Olives weeping while arranging Hushai's return as an informant.

l: Shimei, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Shimei, a Benjamite of Saul's house, son of Gera, living at Bahurim. He curses David and throws stones, blaming him for Saul's house and Absalom's rise; David forbids Abishai to kill him. Later he hurries to meet David at the Jordan with a thousand Benjamites, confesses sin, and David swears he will not die.

l: Shimei’s cursing of David, The Second Book of Samuel
s: has_participant Shimei [cursed and threw stones and dust at David] Shimei curses David and throws stones and dust at him and his servants at Bahurim, calling him a man of blood. Abishai wants to behead Shimei, but David refuses, saying the LORD has invited the cursing and may repay him good for it.

l: woman (of Bahurim), The Second Book of Samuel
s: hides Jonathan [covered the well with crushed grain, with Ahimaaz] The woman of the house in Bahurim spread a covering over the well's mouth and crushed grain on it so nothing was known. She told Absalom's servants that Jonathan and Ahimaaz had gone over the brook of water, so they gave up the search and returned to Jerusalem.

l: well (at Bahurim), The Second Book of Samuel
s: located_at Bahurim [in the court of a man's house] The well in the court of a man's house in Bahurim served as the hiding place for Jonathan and Ahimaaz. It was covered and spread with crushed grain, and the two came up out of it after Absalom's servants left.

l: Amasa, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Amasa, son of Ithra the Israelite, is told by David to gather Judah's men within three days. He overstays, meets Joab at Gibeon's great stone, ignores Joab's sword and is killed; his body is moved off the highway and covered.

l: Barzillai the Gileadite, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Barzillai, an eighty-year-old great Gileadite from Rogelim, sustained David at Mahanaim, then escorts him over the Jordan. He declines David's offer of life in Jerusalem due to age, sends Chimham instead, receives David's kiss and blessing, and returns home.

l: Ahithophel's counsel, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Ahithophel's counsel was good advice to strike David's weary forces that night and kill only the king; it pleased Absalom and the elders, yet the LORD ordained its defeat, so it was not followed.

l: Hushai's counsel, The Second Book of Samuel
s: is_preferred_over Ahithophel's counsel [judged by Absalom and all the men of Israel] Hushai's counsel was to gather all Israel from Dan to Beersheba and have Absalom lead the battle in person, falling on David like dew and dragging any city he entered into the river with ropes. Absalom and all the men of Israel judged it better than Ahithophel's counsel.

l: Ahithophel's suicide, The Second Book of Samuel
s: When Ahithophel saw his counsel was not followed, he went to his city, set his house in order, and hanged himself. He died and was buried in the tomb of his father.

l: Cushite, The Second Book of Samuel
s: The Cushite was told by Joab to go tell the king what he had seen, and he bowed to Joab and ran. He arrived after Ahimaaz, announced that the LORD had avenged the king, and when asked about Absalom answered that the king's enemies should be as that young man is, thereby revealing his death.

l: forest of Ephraim, The Second Book of Samuel
s: The forest of Ephraim was the site of the battle between David's servants and Israel. The battle spread over the whole countryside, and the forest devoured more people that day than the sword did. Absalom was cast into a great pit in the forest and covered with stones.

l: oak (in the forest of Ephraim), The Second Book of Samuel
s: has_attribute great [thick boughs] A great oak with thick boughs caught Absalom's head as his mule passed beneath, leaving him hanging between sky and earth. Joab thrust three darts through Absalom's heart while he was still alive in the oak.

l: battle in the forest of Ephraim, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Battle in the forest of Ephraim where David's forces, in three divisions under Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, defeated Israel; twenty thousand were slain, the forest killing more than the sword, ending when Joab blew the trumpet after Absalom's death.

l: David's mourning for Absalom, The Second Book of Samuel
s: David's lamentation over Absalom's death, in the room over the city gate. Told by the Cushite, he weeps and cries that he wishes he had died instead. His loud grieving turns the day's victory into mourning for the people, until Joab's rebuke makes him rise and sit in the gate.

l: the people, The Second Book of Samuel
s: The people hear that the king grieves for his son, and their victory turns to mourning as they sneak into the city like those ashamed after fleeing a battle. After David sits in the gate they all come before him, and later all the people cross the Jordan with him.

l: David's return to Jerusalem, The Second Book of Samuel
s: David prompts the return by sending Zadok and Abiathar to the elders of Judah, and Judah sends word for him and his servants to return. He comes to the Jordan, where Judah meets him at Gilgal, and he crosses and proceeds to Gilgal, with the account in this unit ending before he reaches Jerusalem.

l: dispute between Israel and Judah over the king, The Second Book of Samuel
s: The men of Israel protest that Judah stole the king away and brought him over the Jordan with his household and men. Judah answers that the king is a close relative and that they gained nothing at his cost, while Israel claims ten parts in him; the quarrel remains unresolved, with Judah's words fiercer.

l: Sheba the son of Bichri, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Sheba, a wicked Benjamite from Ephraim's hill country, rebels against King David by rallying Israel with a trumpet, alarming David; pursued to Abel of Beth Maacah, he is beheaded and his head thrown to Joab.

l: wise woman (of Abel of Beth Maacah), The Second Book of Samuel
s: A wise woman of Abel of Beth Maacah, calls to Joab from the city, pleads that peaceable, faithful Abel not be destroyed, promises Sheba's head, then wisely persuades the people, who behead Sheba.

l: Abel of Beth Maacah, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Abel of Beth Maacah is a city, called a mother in Israel and once known for counsel. Sheba takes refuge there, Joab besieges it, and its people end the siege by killing Sheba.

l: Gibeonites, The Second Book of Samuel
s: The Gibeonites, a remnant of the Amorites bound by Israel's oath, were targeted by Saul. They refuse silver or gold, request seven of Saul's sons, and hang them before the LORD in Gibeah.

l: famine, The Second Book of Samuel
s: A three-year famine in David's days, attributed by the LORD to Saul's bloody killing of the Gibeonites; after atonement and burials, God answers prayer for the land.

l: seven sons of Saul's house, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Seven sons of Saul's house: Armoni, Mephibosheth, and Merab's five sons by Adriel. Delivered to the Gibeonites, they are hanged together on the mountain before the LORD at barley harvest's start; their bones are later buried with Saul and Jonathan's.

l: Ishbibenob, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Ishbibenob, a Philistine son of the giant, wields a three-hundred-shekel bronze spear and new sword, expecting to kill the faint David in battle, but Abishai strikes and kills him.

l: the LORD's theophany (storm and deliverance of David), The Second Book of Samuel
s: In answer to David's cry, the LORD appears in anger amid a storm: earth shakes, fire and smoke issue from him, he rides a cherub on the wind and thunders; arrows and lightning scatter enemies, and he draws David from many waters.

l: David's song of deliverance, The Second Book of Samuel
s: David's song, spoken to the LORD on the day he delivered him from enemies and Saul. It opens with praise and distress, then a storm theophany and David's claimed righteousness, then victory over enemies and rule over nations, closing with thanksgiving and the LORD's lasting kindness to David's offspring.

l: Eleazar, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Eleazar, son of Dodai, is one of David's three mighty men. He fought the Philistines alone until his hand froze to his sword; the LORD gave victory, and Israel returned only for plunder.

l: Shammah the son of Agee, The Second Book of Samuel
s: is_son_of Agee [a Hararite] Shammah the son of Agee, a Hararite, is named as a mighty man. When the people fled from the Philistines gathered at a plot full of lentils, he stood in the middle of the plot, defended it, and killed the Philistines. The LORD worked a great victory.

l: three mighty men, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Three of the thirty chief men came to David at the cave of Adullam at harvest time. They broke through the Philistine army, drew water from the well of Bethlehem by the gate, and brought it to David, who poured it out to the LORD. Eleazar is named among the three, and Abishai was their chief but was not counted as one of them. Benaiah was more honorable than the thirty but did not attain to the three.

l: mighty men of David, The Second Book of Samuel
s: The mighty men are listed by name, led by Josheb Basshebeth, chief of the captains, who killed eight hundred at one time. They include the three, Abishai, Benaiah, and the thirty, ending with Uriah the Hittite and a total of thirty-seven. Their deeds include victories over the Philistines, an Egyptian, and a lion.

l: well of Bethlehem, The Second Book of Samuel
s: The well of Bethlehem is by the gate, and David longs to drink from it. Three mighty men break through the Philistine army to draw water from it and bring it to him.

l: David's last words, The Second Book of Samuel
s: is_spoken_by David David's last words say the LORD's Spirit spoke by him and that a righteous ruler who fears God is like the morning light after rain. He says God made an everlasting covenant with his house, ordered and sure. The ungodly will be like thorns, burned utterly with fire.

l: water offering, The Second Book of Samuel
s: is_poured_out_to LORD [David refused to drink it] When the three mighty men bring David the water from the well of Bethlehem, he will not drink it and pours it out to the LORD. He says it is the blood of men who risked their lives to go.

l: Gad, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Gad is a prophet and David's seer who relays the LORD's word: first offering David three punishments to choose from, then instructing him to build an altar on Araunah the Jebusite's threshing floor.

l: Araunah the Jebusite, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Araunah, a Jebusite who owns a threshing floor, bows to the king, freely offers it with cattle and equipment, but David insists on paying; he sells them for fifty silver shekels.

l: angel (the LORD’s angel), The Second Book of Samuel
s: The LORD's angel, sent as destroyer of the people, stretches his hand toward Jerusalem to destroy it; the LORD says enough, commanding him to withdraw, at Araunah the Jebusite's threshing floor.

l: census of Israel and Judah, The Second Book of Samuel
s: A census of Israel and Judah ordered by David at the LORD's prompting, despite Joab's objection. Spanning the land from across the Jordan to Beersheba, it lasted nine months and twenty days, counting 800,000 in Israel and 500,000 in Judah; David then called it sin and foolishness.

l: pestilence, The Second Book of Samuel
s: A pestilence sent by the LORD on Israel, chosen by David from three options, kills seventy thousand from Dan to Beersheba, is halted before Jerusalem's destruction, and is removed after David's altar offerings.

l: threshing floor of Araunah, The Second Book of Samuel
s: The threshing floor is where the LORD's angel stands when the LORD stops the destruction. Gad directs David to build an altar there, and David buys it with the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.

l: altar (David’s altar to the LORD), The Second Book of Samuel
s: David builds the altar on Araunah's threshing floor at Gad's direction after paying for the site. He offers burnt offerings and peace offerings on it, and the LORD is entreated for the land and the plague is removed from Israel.

These records cover the whole Book of Proverbs, chapters 1 to 31, a collection of wisdom sayings and instructions. It opens by naming the proverbs of Solomon, son of David, and stating their purpose: to give wisdom, instruction and prudence to the simple and young. The central theme is that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, and that wisdom brings life while folly brings ruin. Chapters 1 to 9 are mainly a father's speeches to his son. He urges him to heed instruction, avoid violent sinners, and guard himself against the strange woman or adulteress, whose house leads to death and Sheol. Wisdom is personified as a woman who calls in the streets and gates, promises security and life, and in chapter 8 describes herself as present with the LORD at creation. Chapter 9 sets Wisdom's feast against the foolish woman's invitation, which leads to the depths of Sheol. Chapters 10 to 22 form a long series of short, contrasting sayings about the righteous and the wicked, the wise and the fool, and the diligent and the lazy. They treat speech, correction, wealth and poverty, honest weights, kings and justice, family discipline, and friendship. The LORD is shown as weighing hearts, directing steps, and ruling over human plans. Chapter 22 shifts toward a section of counsel from the wise, claiming thirty sayings so that trust may be in the LORD. Chapters 23 to 24 return to warnings addressed to a son: restraint with rulers, avoiding greed, prostitutes and drunkenness, not envying evil men, rescuing those led to death, and fearing the LORD and the king. Chapter 24 ends with the sluggard's overgrown field. Chapters 25 to 29 are described as further proverbs of Solomon copied by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah. They cover kings, neighbors, fools, sluggards, gossips, boasting, friendship, and the contrast between wicked and righteous rulers, ending with the claim that justice comes from the LORD. The last two chapters are attributed to others. Chapter 30 gives the words of Agur son of Jakeh, who confesses ignorance, affirms that every word of God is flawless, prays to be kept from both poverty and riches, and offers numerical sayings. Chapter 31 gives the words of King Lemuel, taught by his mother, who warns against women and wine and urges just judgment for the poor. The book closes with a poem praising a worthy woman who works diligently, provides for her household, and gives to the poor, concluding that charm and beauty are vain but a woman who fears the LORD shall be praised.

Solomon, son of David and king of Israel, is identified as author of the proverbs, later copied by Hezekiah's men. The Proverbs opening names him as source, offering wisdom, instruction, righteousness, justice and equity.

The LORD is the central divine figure in these records, presented as creator, moral judge, and source of wisdom. At the outset, fear of him is named the beginning of knowledge, and seeking wisdom leads the son to understand that fear and find the knowledge of God. He gives wisdom, with knowledge and understanding coming from his mouth. He stores sound wisdom for the upright, shields those who walk in integrity, and guards the paths of justice. By wisdom he founded the earth and by understanding established the heavens. He set the deep's boundaries and marked out the earth's foundations. He made everything for its own end, and he made the hearing ear and the seeing eye. His moral character is the most developed theme. He loves, befriends, blesses, and delights in the righteous, upright, humble, and those who do the truth. He hears their prayer, keeps widows' borders, and does not let the righteous go hungry. He abominates the wicked, the perverse, lying lips, pride, false balances, and those who justify the wicked or condemn the righteous. Six things, indeed seven, are listed as hateful to him. He curses the wicked's house, mocks mockers, and uproots the house of the proud. He corrects the son as a father corrects a son he delights in. He is all-seeing and all-knowing. His eyes are everywhere, he examines all paths, and he weighs motives, tests hearts, and treats the human spirit as his lamp. He is sovereign: he directs steps, decides the lot, holds the king's heart like watercourses, and holds victory in battle. His counsel prevails, and no wisdom or understanding stands against him. He prefers righteousness and justice to sacrifice. He is Maker of both rich and poor, pleads the poor's case, gives sight to the poor and the oppressor, and counts kindness to the poor as a loan to himself. The records close by calling him a flawless, protective Holy One. His name is a strong tower, those who trust him are kept safe, he shields those who take refuge in him, and he repays each person according to his work. The son is commanded to fear him along with the king, and people are told to wait for him to save rather than repay evil, and not to add to his words.

Wisdom is a personified, woman-like figure in Proverbs who calls aloud at city gates, public squares and high places. She promises security to those who listen and rebukes the simple, mockers and fools who refuse her, saying she will not answer their calls. Her worth exceeds silver, gold and rubies; in her right hand is length of days and in her left riches and honor, her ways are pleasant and her paths peace, and she is a tree of life to those who hold her. The LORD used wisdom to found the earth, and the wise will inherit glory. She then builds a house with seven pillars, prepares meat, wine and a table, and sends out maidens to invite the simple to leave their ways and live. Later the records turn to how wisdom shows in people: on the lips of the discerning, in accepting commandments and correction, and in humility, while pride, despising a neighbor and folly mark its lack. The wise win souls, many counselors bring victory, and the foolish are punished by their own folly. The records close by declaring that getting wisdom is far better than gold and that understanding is a fountain of life.

The son is the addressee of a father figure's instruction, repeatedly called 'my son' across Proverbs. He is a learner who receives commands, warnings, and promises. Early on he is told to heed his father's instruction and his mother's teaching, and not to follow enticing sinners. Next he is urged to seek wisdom and understanding, which will bring the fear of the LORD and deliverance from evil men and the strange woman, and to walk the path of the righteous. Then he is told to keep the commandments, trust the LORD rather than his own understanding, honor the LORD, accept discipline, and do good to his neighbor, with promises of long life, peace, favor, health, and plenty. Later he is told to show restraint, accept correction, avoid drunkenness, gluttony, and sexual temptation, and buy truth, with a hope that will not be cut off. Finally he is told to fear the LORD and the king, not to envy evildoers or join rebels, to judge impartially, to refuse revenge, to rescue those led to death, and to prepare his fields before building his house.

l: father and mother (of the son), Proverbs
s: A father and mother, who gave life to and bore the son, are urged to be honored, not despised in old age. They rejoice and delight when the son is wise and righteous, and the speaker's heart rejoices with them.

l: sinners (those who entice the son), Proverbs
s: Sinners invite the son to lie in wait for the innocent, shed blood, seize wealth and share one purse with them. The text says their feet run to evil and that they in fact lie in wait for their own blood and lives.
The simple are a group who love simplicity and are questioned by Wisdom; backsliding will kill them, yet they gain wisdom when the mocker is punished, and proverbs offer prudence.

Fools are portrayed as despising wisdom, instruction and knowledge, and detesting turning from evil. Chapter 1 warns their careless ease destroys them and they reap their own schemes; Chapter 13 adds that they expose folly and harm companions.

A wise person is portrayed in Chapter 14 as building a house, thinking carefully about their way, fearing and shunning evil, and being slow to anger; their lips protect them, riches crown them, and the king favors them.

Wisdom is the central subject of these Proverbs passages: a prized quality that the foolish despise and that is too high for a fool. It is to be sought like silver and hidden treasure, bought and not sold, even at the cost of all one's possessions, with the LORD as its giver. The records open with wisdom and instruction as the proverbs' goal, with parental teaching likened to a garland of grace. Next, when wisdom enters a son's heart, knowledge becomes pleasant and she guards him from evil. She is called supreme; if she is loved, esteemed, embraced and not forsaken, she preserves, keeps, exalts and honors a person, giving a garland of grace and crown of splendor, and she is life itself. Further on, the son must apply heart and ears, accept correction, and a wise heart gladdens his parents. Finally, wisdom builds a house and fills its rooms with treasure, gives a wise man great power, brings victory through many advisors, and is compared to honey, sweet to the soul, bringing a reward and a hope that will not be cut off.

Sheol is the realm of departed spirits, where the foolish woman's guests lie in its depths and which lies open to the LORD's sight. Chapter 30 lists it among things never satisfied, alongside the barren womb, thirsty earth, and fire.

takes_away life of its owners Greed and violent plunder appear in the sinners' scheme to ambush the innocent and fill their houses with loot. The text says such ways take away the life of those who are greedy for gain, as the plunderers ambush their own lives.

keeps my son [protective role] Understanding is something the son is to call out for and lift his voice for, and the LORD's mouth is its source. It will keep the son and deliver him from the way of evil and from the strange woman, and it brings knowledge of righteousness, justice, equity and every good path.

gives teaching and commandments [to the son] The speaker calls on his son, and then his sons, to listen to his wisdom and understanding and not depart from the words of his mouth. He warns against the adulteress, describes the regret that follows ignoring instruction, and commends faithful love to his wife. He frames his teaching as the instruction whose lack leads to death.

The righteous are a group portrayed as secure and favored. They hold just thoughts, are cautious in friendship, and respect their animals' lives. Their root stays unmoved and flourishing, their house stands, and they escape trouble, suffering no mischief. They obtain the LORD's favor and dwell in the land. The way of righteousness is described as life, with no death in its path.

The wicked are a group defined by perverse speech, abandoning upright paths for darkness, delighting in evil, and crooked ways. They are treacherous and destined to be rooted out of the land. Their own wickedness brings them down; they take the righteous's place in trouble, destroy neighbors with their mouths, earn deceitful wages, expect wrath, and will not go unpunished. Trust in riches fails them, and they are ultimately repaid.

The strange woman, also called the foreigner or adulteress, is a figure of seduction who appears across four chapters and is set against Wisdom. In Chapters 2 and 5 she flatters with words, forsakes the friend of her youth, and forgets the covenant of her God. Her lips drip honey and her mouth is smoother than oil, but in the end she is bitter as wormwood and sharp as a two-edged sword. Her house, feet and steps lead down to death and Sheol; none who go to her return or reach the paths of life. Her ways are crooked without her knowing it, and the son is told to be delivered from her and not to come near her house. In Chapter 7 she meets a young man in the street dressed as a prostitute, crafty, loud and defiant, lurking in streets and squares. She kisses him, claims to have paid her vows, and invites him to her perfumed bed since her husband is away until the full moon. Her flattering words lead him astray, and the speaker says she has thrown down many wounded and all her slain are a mighty army. In Chapter 8 the contrast is made through Wisdom, who cries out publicly, speaks truth, hates evil, and offers counsel, power, riches and honor. Kings and rulers reign by her; the LORD possessed her before creation. She was his craftsman and delight, and whoever finds her finds life, while those who hate her love death.

l: the fear of the LORD, Proverbs
s: The fear of the LORD is a virtue that prolongs days and is better than great revenues gained through injustice, even when one's own possessions are little; it aligns with righteousness and departing from evil.

The wicked are portrayed as a class of people defined by habitual evil. They cannot rest unless they do wrong, living on the bread of wickedness and wine of violence, walking a dark path where they stumble unknowingly. Their advice is deceitful, their mercies cruel, their mouths gush evil, and their hearts plot violence and desire plunder. They respond to reproof with abuse. Their sacrifices and ways are an abomination to the LORD, who is far from them, and their income brings trouble. The portrait moves from their habits and darkness, to their deceit and misleading way, to their standing before the LORD, and finally to their end: overthrown by calamity, with no reward and a snuffed-out lamp. The son is warned not to envy them, and whoever calls them righteous is cursed.

The righteous are people guided by integrity, delivered from trouble through knowledge, and desiring only good. They flourish like a green leaf, bear a tree of life, reap sure reward and life, and their offspring are delivered.

Instruction, which comes from the LORD and is not to be despised, is a life-or-death matter. Chapter 5 shows a son who hated instruction and regrets it at his end, and the wicked die for lacking it. Chapter 15 adds that the prudent and wise heed reproof and live, while scoffers and fools who refuse it face death and gain no understanding.

The father urges his sons to listen to his instruction and not forsake his law, recalling that he was once a tender only child taught by his own father. He says he has taught them in the way of wisdom and led them in straight paths. He commands them to keep their hearts, avoid the path of the wicked, and turn away from evil.

The sons are told to listen, receive the father's sayings, get wisdom and understanding, and hold firmly to instruction. They are warned not to enter the path of the wicked and are told to guard their hearts, put away a perverse mouth, look straight ahead, and not turn to the right or left. If they obey, the years of their life will be many and their steps will not be hampered.

The righteous are people who walk a path likened to dawning light growing toward perfect day, contrasting the wicked's darkness. They hate lies, are guarded by righteousness, shine brightly, and are rewarded with prosperity, satisfaction, and the sinner's stored wealth.

give life [to those who keep them] The speaker tells his son to keep his words and commandments, to lay them up within him, and to guard his teaching as the apple of his eye. He is to bind them on his fingers and write them on the tablet of his heart, and the text says that keeping the commandments brings life.

The son is told to pay attention to the speaker's wisdom, keep away from the adulteress, and not come near the door of her house. He is warned that otherwise he will lose his honor, years, and wealth, and will groan at the end, regretting that he despised instruction. He is urged to drink from his own cistern, rejoice in the wife of his youth, and be captivated always by her love.

The wife of the son's youth is portrayed as his exclusive, rightful source of satisfaction, likened to a loving doe and graceful deer. He is urged to rejoice in her, be satisfied by her breasts always, and be captivated by her love.

A topic contrasting adultery and fidelity: adultery brings death, ruin, and loss of honor, years, and wealth to strangers, while fidelity is pictured as drinking from one's own cistern and rejoicing in the wife of one's youth, closing with a rhetorical question to the son.
The ant, a creature with no chief, overseer, or ruler, is a provident model of wisdom: it stores bread in summer and gathers food in harvest, urging the sluggard to learn.

The sluggard is a habitually idle, oversleeping man who lacks understanding and offers excuses, such as claiming a lion is outside. He is told to consider the ant. His field and vineyard are neglected. Across both chapters, a little sleep and folded hands bring poverty and want, arriving suddenly like a robber or an armed man.
A worthless man of iniquity with a perverse mouth and heart, who winks and gestures while continually devising evil and sowing discord, and who therefore faces sudden, irreparable calamity.
A seductive immoral woman with flattering tongue and captivating eyelids; a son is warned against lusting after her beauty because she ruins a man to a bread crust and hunts his precious life.
A husband's wife, forbidden to adulterers; touching her is like scooping fire into one's lap, and the offender will not go unpunished.
A man who commits adultery is called void of understanding, destroying his own soul; he suffers wounds and lasting dishonor, and the jealous husband will show no mercy, refusing ransom or gifts.

results_in entrapment by one's words Becoming collateral or striking hands in pledge for a neighbor or stranger is described as a trap, ensnaring the son by the words of his mouth. He is urged to act immediately, giving no sleep to his eyes, to escape it.

A list of seven things the LORD hates, called abominations in Chapter 6: arrogant eyes, a lying tongue, innocent-blood-shedding hands, a heart devising wicked schemes, feet swift to mischief, a lying false witness, and one who sows discord among brothers.

A father's commandment and mother's teaching, which a son must keep bound on his heart and neck. They guide him walking, watch him sleeping, and talk with him waking. Called a lamp, light, and the way of life, they protect him from the immoral woman.

Adultery is likened to carrying fire or walking on coals: unavoidably harmful. Committed without understanding, it destroys the soul, brings wounds and lasting dishonor, and provokes the husband's vengeance, unlike a hungry thief's forgivable theft.

The speaker addresses his son, urging him to keep his words and commandments and to call wisdom his sister. He recounts watching from his lattice window as a young man was seduced, then turns to his sons with a warning to avoid the strange woman's paths because her house leads to death.

The young man is seen among the simple ones, passing near the strange woman's corner and heading toward her house in the twilight. She catches and seduces him, and he follows her immediately like an ox going to slaughter or a bird hurrying to a snare, not knowing it will cost his life.

Wisdom and understanding are a topic first presented as kin: in Chapter 7 the son is told to call wisdom his sister and understanding his relative, guarding him from the strange woman's flattery. In Chapter 9, wisdom begins with fear of the LORD, understanding is knowledge of the Holy One, and wisdom promises longer life.

is_blessed_when keeping wisdom's ways The sons of mankind, including the simple and fools, are addressed by wisdom's voice and urged to gain prudence, understanding, and instruction rather than silver or gold. Wisdom's delight was with the sons of men, and she calls them to listen. Those who hear and watch daily at her gates are blessed and find life, while those who sin against her wrong their own souls.

has_part sea boundary [set by the LORD so waters don't violate his commandment] The earth, along with the deeps, springs, mountains, hills, fields, and dust of the world, is described as not yet existing when wisdom was born. When the LORD established the heavens, set the sea's boundary so the waters would not violate his commandment, and marked out the earth's foundations, wisdom was present as craftsman by his side.

The foolish woman is loud, undisciplined and ignorant. She sits at her door in the city's high places, mimicking Wisdom's call to the simple with stolen water and secret food, but her guests end up in Sheol's depths.

The simple, described as void of understanding, are invited by Wisdom to turn in, eat and drink, leave their simple ways, and live. The foolish woman calls them with the same words, and the one who follows her does not know that her guests are the departed spirits in Sheol.
A scoffer who answers correction with insult and hates those who reprove him; Chapter 9 warns correcting him invites abuse, and he alone bears his mocking's consequences.
A wise person who loves the one reproving him and grows wiser when instructed; like the righteous, he increases in learning, benefiting himself.

Wisdom's feast consists of prepared meat, mixed wine, a set table, and bread, offered to the simple and those void of understanding. Those who partake are urged to leave their simple ways, live, and walk in the way of understanding.

The upright and righteous are portrayed as a group whose righteousness delivers them from death. They are blessed and well remembered; their mouths are a spring of life, their labor leads to life, and their desires are granted. They stand firm forever and are never removed. They fear the LORD, walk in uprightness, enjoy good will, and their tent flourishes. The evil bow before them, and in death they have refuge.

The wicked are portrayed as people whose treasures profit nothing and whose names rot. Fears overtake them, hope perishes, years shorten, and violence covers their mouths. They bring shame, fall to their own wickedness, and their lamp is snuffed out. Hunger and misfortune pursue them, and their wealth is stored up for the righteous.

Fools are a type portrayed across Chapters 10 and 12: their mouths are near ruin, they take pleasure in wickedness, and they die for lack of understanding. Later they hate reproof, consider their own way right, show annoyance at once, and proclaim foolishness from the heart.
The wise in heart accept commandments, store up knowledge, and restrain their lips; a wise son gladdens his father and finds pleasure in wisdom.

Righteousness is set against wickedness throughout the chapter: righteousness delivers from death, leads to life and brings blessing, while wickedness profits nothing, leads to sin and ends in perishing. Treasures of wickedness profit nothing, and the way of the LORD is a stronghold for the upright but destruction for those who do iniquity.

has_characteristic multitude of words brings disobedience [restraint is wise] Speech marks character in this unit. The righteous mouth is a spring of life, choice silver and a source of wisdom that feeds many, while a perverse tongue is cut off. Hidden hatred, slander and many words bring harm, and restraining the lips is wise.

Correction and discipline: heeded by those on the way of life, the rod of correction gives wisdom. Chapter 29 warns the stiff-necked are suddenly destroyed, correction brings peace, and pampered servants end badly.

delivers_from death [righteousness] Righteousness delivers from death, directs a person's way and yields a sure reward and life, while wickedness brings death, treachery, trapping by evil desires and downfall. Those who seek good find favor, and evil comes to those who search for it. Riches do not profit in the day of wrath.

Wealth and riches: they ransom a man's life, yet are deceptive in appearance; dishonest gain dwindles while steady gathering grows; riches lack profit in the day of wrath, and a sinner's wealth is stored for the righteous.

The neighbor is a proverb-style figure: disputes should be argued with him privately, not rushed to court, and his confidences kept lest the betrayer suffer lasting shame. Visits should be infrequent to avoid his hatred, and false testimony against him is likened to a weapon.

A contrast between generosity and withholding: the one who scatters and waters others increases and is blessed, while the one who withholds more than appropriate gains poverty and is cursed; mercy benefits one's own soul.
A wise person heeds counsel, speaks healing words, is commended according to wisdom, and prudently overlooks insults while keeping knowledge.
Diligent people are a group who rule, have plenty of bread from tilling their land, and hold prized possessions, in contrast to slothful people who end in slave labor.
A false witness lies, mocks justice, and gulps down iniquity; the records state repeatedly that such a witness will not go unpunished, ending in the fate of perishing.

Speech's power to destroy or heal: wicked words ambush for blood and rash words pierce, while upright and wise speech rescues and heals. Truthful lips last forever, lies only a moment, and kind words gladden anxious hearts; one's mouth brings good or entraps.

listens_to father [instruction] The wise son listens to his father's instruction, in contrast to the scoffer who ignores rebuke. A good man is also said to leave an inheritance to his children's children.
does_not_listen_to discipline and instruction [rebuke] The scoffer does not listen to rebuke, in contrast to the wise son who heeds his father's instruction.
Wisdom is a topic in Chapter 13: the wise's teaching is a life-giving spring turning people from death's snares; it grows by walking with the wise and taking advice.

Chapter 13 teaching on discipline: despising instruction brings poverty and shame, while respecting commands and heeding correction rewards and honors the wise; loving parents carefully discipline their children.

The fool is a figure of self-destructive folly: he demolishes his own house, earns a rod through his speech, mocks atonement, and is hot-headed, reckless, and deceitful. Chapter 14 concludes by advising people to avoid him, since his lips hold no knowledge.

The wicked are perverse people who despise the LORD, yet bow at the gates of the righteous. Made for the day of evil, they go astray, are repaid for their ways, and finally are brought down in calamity as their house is overthrown.

The poor and needy are shunned even by neighbors while the rich keep friends; despising neighbors is sin, pitying the poor brings blessing, and oppressing them scorns their Maker while kindness honors him.

Wisdom is built into the house, sought in vain by the scoffer but easy for the discerning, and it rests in the heart of those with understanding. Folly tears down the house, is inherited by the simple, and crowns fools with folly. The chapter sets the two against each other, as the prudent are crowned with knowledge and the quick-tempered display folly.
The wise commend and spread knowledge, gladden their fathers as wise sons, seek counsel, keep straight ways, and follow a life path upward, away from Sheol.
Fools are people who gush out and feed on folly, fail to spread knowledge, and despise their father's correction and their mother.

The righteous are a group whose house holds much treasure and whose hearts weigh answers; the LORD delights in their prayer, hears them, and loves those pursuing righteousness, their path like a highway.

turns_away wrath A gentle answer turns away wrath, in contrast to a harsh word that stirs up anger. A gentle tongue is called a tree of life, and a word spoken at the right time is called good and brings joy.

The king is portrayed as a ruler whose throne rests on righteousness; he speaks inspired judgments, delights in righteous lips and truth-speakers, abhors wrongdoing, and holds power of life and death: his wrath brings death, his favor brings life like spring rain.

pacifies king's wrath The wise man pacifies the king's wrath. The wise in heart are called prudent, their heart instructs their mouth and adds learning to their lips, and their pleasant words are like a honeycomb, sweet to the soul and healing to the bones.

precedes destruction Everyone proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD and will not go unpunished. Pride goes before destruction and an arrogant spirit before a fall, so it is better to be lowly among the poor than to share plunder with the proud.

The fool, portrayed in Chapter 17, is someone who cannot benefit from wisdom: he lacks understanding, so money cannot buy it, and rebuke affects him less than lashes affect the wise. His eyes wander without focus, he is unfit for excellent speech, and he grieves his parents. Encountering him in his folly is worse than meeting a robbed bear, yet silence makes him seem wise.

A wicked person heeds wicked lips, secretly takes bribes to pervert justice, and seeks only rebellion. The outcome is judgment: a cruel messenger will be sent against him, and evil, trouble, and no prosperity follow those repaying evil for good.

The person of understanding has wisdom before his face, responds more deeply to rebuke than a fool to a hundred lashes, spares his words, stays even tempered, and is thought discerning; a wise servant may even rule a shameful son.

Strife is portrayed as worse than a feast, since quiet with a dry morsel is better. It begins like breaching a dam, so it should be stopped early; it is loved by those who love disobedience, and repetition separates friends.

The fool rejects understanding and prefers voicing his own opinion; this speech brings strife and beatings, ultimately ruining him and ensnaring his soul. Answering before listening is labeled folly and shame.

The LORD's righteous are a group, spoken of as a man, who find safety by running to the LORD's name, a strong tower, unlike the rich whose wealth is imagined protection. Later, the wicked are warned not to attack his home; he falls seven times yet rises, while they fall to calamity.

Speech, likened to deep waters, holds power over death and life, and those who love it eat its fruit. A person is filled and satisfied by the harvest of their lips, while gossip's words sink deep and a fool's speech brings strife and ruin.

is_compared_to flowing brook [fountain of wisdom] The fountain of wisdom is compared to a flowing brook. The ear of the wise seeks knowledge and the heart of the discerning gets it, and humility is said to come before honor.

The poor man who walks in integrity is valued above the perverse fool and the liar, yet he is abandoned: separated from friends, shunned by all relatives, and avoided despite pleas. Whoever pities him lends to the LORD and is rewarded.

The fool is a perverse-speaking figure whose foolishness subverts his own way and whose heart rages against the LORD; unfit for delicate living, he is destined for beatings, and as a son he calamitously burdens his father.

benefits the one who gets it [loves his own soul and finds good] He who gets wisdom loves his own soul, and he who keeps understanding will find good. Listening to counsel and receiving instruction makes one wise in the latter end. A man's discretion makes him slow to anger, and rebuking one with understanding leads him to gain knowledge.

The sluggard is a archetype of laziness portrayed across two chapters. He is so idle he buries his hand in the dish and won't bring food to his mouth, turns on his bed like a door on its hinges, and invents excuses such as a lion in the road. Slothfulness brings deep sleep, hunger, and death by his own desire, yet he deems himself wiser than seven discreet men.

A son portrayed in proverb-like records: a foolish son is his father's calamity, and one who robs his father and drives away his mother brings shame. Yet he should be disciplined because there is hope, and warned against abandoning instruction and straying from knowledge.

is_prepared_for scoffer Parents are told to discipline a son for there is hope, and not to be a willing party to his death. Penalties are prepared for scoffers and beatings for fools, and flogging a scoffer teaches the simple prudence. The hot-tempered man must pay the penalty, and rescuing him means doing it again.

A king whose terror resembles a lion's roar; provoking him costs one's life. On his judgment throne he scatters evil with his eyes, and when wise winnows out the wicked. Love and faithfulness keep him safe and sustain his throne.

The fool is a quarreling figure described in Chapter 26 as unfit for honor, needing a rod for his back, and making parables useless in his mouth. He repeats his folly like a dog returning to its vomit. Advice is paradoxical: answer him, or not, according to his folly. There is more hope for him than for one wise in his own eyes.
The sluggard is a proverbial lazy figure who refuses to plow because of winter, then begs at harvest with nothing; a related warning links loving sleep to poverty.

is_an_abomination_to the LORD Differing weights and differing measures are called, both alike, an abomination to the LORD. The chapter repeats the point by saying the LORD detests differing weights and that dishonest scales are not pleasing.

A righteous man who walks in integrity is described as leaving blessed children after him. The chapter contrasts this with the many who claim unfailing love, asking who can find a faithful man, and with the buyer who calls goods no good and then boasts. It also condemns fraudulent food, dishonest scales, and differing weights and measures.

The wicked are proud, violent, devious people who desire evil and show neighbors no mercy. They refuse to do right, so their own violence drives them away. Their sacrifices are abominations, and they harden their faces. They end in ruin, serving as a ransom for the righteous.

The righteous are a group who delight in justice and give generously without withholding; the Righteous One brings the wicked to ruin, while the righteous are ransomed by them and the upright establish their ways.

The wise are a group who accept instruction and gain knowledge, keep precious treasure and oil at home, and ultimately scale the mighty's city, toppling its confident strength, unlike the foolish who squander.

is_followed_by the righteous [pursuers find life, righteousness and honor] Doing righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice. It is joy to the righteous but destruction to workers of iniquity, and whoever follows righteousness and kindness finds life, righteousness, and honor.

rule_over the poor The rich share with the poor the fact that the LORD made them all. They rule over the poor, and one who gives to the rich in order to increase his own wealth comes to poverty. Good name and loving favor are said to be better than riches.

The poor are made by the LORD just as the rich are, and they are ruled over by the rich. The text forbids exploiting them because they are poor or crushing them in court. The LORD will plead their case, and one who shares food with them is blessed, while one who oppresses them for gain comes to poverty.

is_more_desirable_than great riches A good name is declared more desirable than great riches, and loving favor is better than silver and gold. This opens the chapter as a value to be preferred over wealth.

Chapter 22 teaches child training and discipline: training a child in the way he should go means he won't depart from it when old, while folly bound in a child's heart is driven far away by the rod of discipline.

A teaching of wise counsel: the reader is urged to listen and apply his heart, since it is pleasant kept within and ready on the lips. Its purpose is trust in the LORD; thirty sayings of knowledge enable sound answers to senders.

offers dainties [deceitful food] The ruler is the host at a meal where the son is warned to consider carefully what is before him and not to desire his dainties, which are called deceitful food. Wealth and the ruler's table are treated as things not to crave.

Wine is portrayed as tempting when red, sparkling and smooth, but warned against: it ultimately bites like a snake and poisons like a viper, bringing woe to those who linger over it or seek mixed wine.

Drunkenness, paired with gluttony, is a warning topic: it brings poverty and rags through drowsiness, then woe, strife, bruises and bloodshot eyes. The drinker sees strange things, feels confused like a sleeper at sea, ignores blows, and wakes only to seek more drink.

has_state overgrown with thorns [covered with nettles, wall broken down] The sluggard's field and vineyard are seen to be completely overgrown with thorns, covered on the surface with nettles, with the stone wall broken down. The narrator considers this well and takes it as instruction about the consequences of idleness.

Kings are portrayed as rulers who find glory in searching out matters, with hearts unsearchable like heaven and earth. Their thrones are established in righteousness by removing the wicked from their presence. The records end by advising humble approach and patience, since rulers can be persuaded.

Wise speech and conduct is likened to apples of gold in silver settings: fitly spoken words, wise reproof, and faithful messengers bring value. It includes patience and a soft tongue that persuade, then urges restraint and kindness to a hungry enemy, which the LORD rewards.

l: man wise in his own eyes, Proverbs
s: has_hope less than a fool The man wise in his own eyes is mentioned in a rhetorical question. The text states there is more hope for a fool than for him.

kindles strife [as coals to embers and wood to fire] The contentious man is compared to coals for hot embers and wood for fire, because he kindles strife. The text notes that a quarrel dies down without gossip, as a fire goes out for lack of wood.

A malicious man masks his hatred with smooth lips while harboring evil in his heart; his charming speech is untrustworthy because of seven abominations within, and his concealed deceit will eventually be exposed publicly in the assembly.

is_repeated_by fool [like a dog returning to its vomit] Folly is the basis for the contradictory instructions on answering a fool, either to avoid becoming like him or to keep him from being wise in his own eyes. The fool repeats his folly like a dog returning to its vomit.
A fool, characterized in Chapter 27 as a source of provocation heavier than stone or sand, whose foolishness is incurable, remaining even if ground in a mortar with grain.

A friend is portrayed as one whose wounds are faithful, unlike an enemy's profuse kisses. Friends give earnest counsel that brings joy and sharpen one another like iron. The reader is finally urged never to forsake his friend or his father's friend.
Flocks and herds are livestock an owner must attend to carefully, since riches do not last forever. Lambs supply clothing, goats can buy a field, and goats' milk feeds the family and servant girls.

The wicked are a group marked by needless fear, mutual praise among law-forsakers, and ignorance of justice. Their rise makes men hide; those who mislead the upright fall into their own trap, and when they perish the righteous thrive.
The righteous are bold as lions, contend with the wicked, and stay safe walking blamelessly; their triumph brings great glory, and they thrive when the wicked perish.

The poor are a group valued for integrity, judged better than perverse rich people, and the understanding poor see through the rich. Oppressing them is condemned; giving to them brings no lack, while ignoring them brings many curses.

is_wise_in own eyes [disposition] The rich man is described as wise in his own eyes, yet the discerning poor see through him. A rich person who is perverse in his ways is judged worse than a poor person of integrity.
A wicked ruler over helpless people is likened to a roaring lion or charging bear; such tyranny reflects lack of judgment, contrasted with those hating ill-gotten gain who live long.
The law is kept by the righteous, who wisely contend with the wicked, while forsakers praise the wicked; whoever refuses to hear it finds even his prayer deemed an abomination.

A proverbial theme on wealth and poverty: wealth from excessive interest ends up with one who pities the poor, greedy haste goes punished, diligent land-work yields food, while fantasy-chasing and stinginess bring unforeseen poverty.

The righteous are a group who care about justice for the poor. They thrive, cause people to rejoice, and sing with gladness. They will see the wicked fall, while dishonest people detest them and the upright detest those people in turn.
The wicked are a group who disregard knowledge; when they rule, people groan, and when they multiply, sin increases. Ensnared by their own sin, the bloodthirsty hate the upright and seek their lives.
A fool habitually vents all his anger, raging or scoffing against a wise man in court so no peace remains; yet he is said to hold more hope than a man hasty in words.
A wise man who controls himself and turns away anger, loves wisdom and brings his father joy, yet finds no peace dealing with a fool in court.

A king whose rule depends on his conduct: justice stabilizes the land and fair judgment of the poor establishes his throne forever, while bribes tear the land down and listening to lies brings wicked officials; justice comes from the LORD.

receives fair judgment from a king [leads to an enduring throne] The righteous care about justice for the poor, and a king who judges the poor fairly will have his throne established. The poor man and the oppressor share this in common: the LORD gives sight to both.
A son who, when corrected with the rod, gains wisdom and gives his parents peace and delight, whereas one left uncorrected shames his mother.

is_cared_about_by the righteous [justice for the poor] Justice by the king makes the land stable, and the righteous care about justice for the poor. Though many seek the ruler's favor, a man's justice comes from the LORD.

l: Agur the son of Jakeh, Proverbs
s: Agur, son of Jakeh, is a speaker of a revelation addressed to Ithiel and Ucal. He calls himself the most ignorant of men, lacking knowledge of the Holy One. He asks who ascended to heaven, affirms God's flawless words, prays against falsehood, poverty and riches, then gives numerical sayings and a closing warning about wrath.
Agur's prayer in Chapter 30 weighs poverty against riches: fullness risks denying God, poverty risks stealing and dishonoring His name, so he asks only for needed food, neither extreme.

A group of wicked generations in four kinds: one that curses its father and withholds blessing from its mother, one pure in its own eyes yet unwashed, one arrogant with lofty eyes, and one that devours the poor and needy with teeth like swords. It closes with a warning that the eye mocking a father is eaten by ravens and eagles.

A saying in Chapter 30 where Agur declares three things too amazing, and four beyond his understanding: the way of an eagle in the air, a serpent on a rock, a ship in the middle of the sea, and a man with a maiden. It closes with the adulterous woman who eats, wipes her mouth, and denies wrongdoing.

l: things the earth cannot bear, Proverbs
s: A proverbial list in Chapter 30 of four things the earth trembles under and cannot bear: a servant who becomes king, a fool filled with food, an unloved woman who marries, and a servant who inherits from her mistress.

A group of four little but exceedingly wise creatures: ants storing food in summer, hyraxes building houses in rocks, locusts advancing in ranks without a king, and a lizard, easily caught yet present in kings' palaces.
A group of four stately marchers listed in Chapter 30: the lion, mightiest among animals and turning away for none; the greyhound; the male goat; and finally the king no one rises against.
